question.leadin: Answer the following about famous archaeological finds in Egypt.
question.text: This British archaeologist led the 1922 excavation of King Tut's tomb in the Valley of the Kings, with funding from Lord Carnavon.
question.clue: Starting at age 17, this person worked for Gaston Maspero, who provided a recommendation for a later employer.

swap.leadin: This ruler of the 19th Dynasty was portrayed in a unique art style in which his hips were not turned.
swap.text: Name this husband of Nefertiti who established a capital at Amarna. He tried to abandon polytheism as the state religion, but ultimately failed.
swap.clue: His wife was the daughter of Ay and he constructed many temples near Karnak to a certain solar god.

question.leadin: This ruler's capital at Amarna was discovered by Flinders Petrie, and his wife was Nefertiti.
question.text: Name this 18th dynasty pharaoh who attempted to establish monotheistic sun worship.
question.clue: Like his father, who married a non-royal woman named Tiy, he married a woman who was not of royal blood, the daughter of a vizier named Ay.

swap.text: This young pharaoh, the son of Akhenaten, had his tomb excavated by Howard Carter.
swap.clue: Arthur Conan Doyle suggested Lord Carnavon's death was caused by "elementals" produced by this man's priests.

question.leadin: This city was built on the site of the ancient city of Rhacotis.
question.text: Name this city, the largest in the world by 200 BCE. The Musaeum, an academic institution based in this city, was the source of the modern word "museum" and also encompassed this city's famous Great Library.
question.clue: In 1477, the Citadel of Qaitbay was constructed using the remains of one of this city's most famous landmarks.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about historical objects.
swap.text: This object was unearthed by Jean-Francois Bouchard in 1799 in Egypt. It contains text written in Greek, Demotic, and Hieroglyphics.
swap.clue: That rediscovery occurred in 1799 while the French soldier Pierre-Francois Bouchard was on the Napoleonic campaign in Egypt.

question.text: This ruler of the Third Dynasty had his architect Imhotep constructed a step pyramid for him, the first of the Egyptian pyramids.
question.clue: An official of this pharaoh communes with the god Khnum to stop a seven-year flood, as recorded on the Famine Stela.

swap.leadin: In ancient Egypt, the vizier was the head official and top advisor in the pharaoh's court.
swap.text: Perhaps the most significant early vizier was this man, who served under Djoser. Best known for his architectural work during his life, he was later deified as the god of medicine.
swap.clue: The great Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara is attributed to this minister and polymath, later deified as a god of medicine, who also completed projects abandoned by Sekhemkhet.

question.leadin: In 1923, a Harlem newspaper alleged a cover-up about this man's skin color.
question.text: Name this man who owned an iron dagger made from a meteorite. A blockbuster exhibit on the "treasures" of this ruler at the Met in the 1970s benefited the Philae temple complex.
question.clue: This son of Akhenaten was buried in the Valley of Kings, in a tomb that was eventually designated KV62.

swap.text: This pharaoh commanded the Egyptian forces at Kadesh. The temples at Abu Simbel were built during his reign.
swap.clue: This husband of Nefertari and successor to Seti I signed the known first peace treaty in history.

question.text: Under Buyid control, the Abbasids were weakened when forced to effectively replace this senior minister with the "emir of emirs." The Ottomans later adopted a "grand" version of this title for their highest ranking official.
question.clue: Stepping stones to this higher office held by Hemiunu included "High Steward" and "Fan-bearer on the Right Side of the King."

swap.text: This Egyptian historian may have conflated Tut with king Rathotis. He wrote the Aegyptiaca during the Ptolemaic era and among other claims, suggested the pharaoh Menes was killed by a hippopotamus.
swap.clue: Continuations of this priest's historical work have been written by the Libyan Apion and Chaeremon.

question.text: Rome formed the province of Arabia Petraea after the death of a king with this epithet, Rabbel II. Ptolemy I also had this epithet which means "savior."
question.clue: Instead of being directly venerating kings as gods, Hellenistic ruler-cults often made offerings to the king under Greek title, which translates as "savior." It was given to the first ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty.

swap.leadin: This ruler, who was the sponsor for the mathematician Euclid, acquired a name meaning "savior" after he established his namesake dynasty in Egypt.
swap.text: Name this ruler who built the Library at Alexandria and is the possible half-brother of Alexander the Great.
swap.clue: This person had Cleomenes of Naucratis killed supposedly since he was "a friend of Perdiccas, and therefore no friend of his".

question.text: The so-called "0 Dynasty" ends and the First Dynasty begins with Narmer unifying these two regions. The Narmer Palette found at Hierakonpolis shows him wearing the red and white crowns of these two regions.
question.answerHtml: Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt [accept Upper and Lower Egypt; accept the Sedge and the Bee]
question.clue: One of them had a name meaning "Land of the Reeds," the other was called the "Land of the North," and the two were collectively called Tawy("tah-wee").

swap.leadin: Herodotus claimed the thickness of Egyptian skulls at this battle was explained by not wearing turbans, and noted that Polycrates of Samos sent forty warships of unreliable scoundrels to take part.
swap.text: Name this 525 BC battle in which the Egyptian Psamtik III fell after the Greek general Phanes directed the Persians to some Arabs who helped them cross the Sinai desert.

question.leadin: Seti I fought a war against these people, whom he called the "Tjehnu," and the Great Karnak Inscription describes the defeat of their "Great Chief" Meryey's alliance with the Lukka and four Sea Peoples.
question.text: Name this people, who at one point ruled Egypt in a dynasty descended from Osorkon the Elder. A stele recounting one pharaoh's victory over these people is also one of the first documents to mention the word "Israel."

swap.text: The greatest monarch of the Middle Kingdom, he built the mortuary complex known to Herodotus as the Labyrinth during his reign in the 19th century BC.
swap.clue: This pharaoh who ordered the construction of the unfinished Black Pyramid and a trap-laden mortuary temple at Hawara, and is best-known for completing a canal to link the Nile with Lake Moeris in the al-Fayyum depression.

question.leadin: This woman invented an early double-boiler, now culinarily referred to as this woman's namesake bath.
question.text: Identify this first-century woman, who Zosimos of Panopolis regarded as the first alchemist in the Western world. She is known for a namesake alchemical axiom stating "One becomes two, two becomes three, and out of the third comes the one as the fourth."
question.answerHtml: Mary the Jewess [accept Mary the Prophetess; accept Maria the Copt; accept Maria Hebraea; accept Maria Prophetissa; accept Māriyya al-Qibṭiyya; prompt on Mary alone]

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the end of the Old Kingdom, FTPE.
swap.text: Toward the very end of the Old Kingdom, the Pyramid Texts began to be replaced by these religious texts, as exemplified by discoveries at the Balat necropolis. In general, they made the afterlife more accessible to commoners than the Pyramid Texts.
